title: Microchips and Semiconductors
summary: The tiny switches that run the modern world: what semiconductors are, how transistors make logic gates, how chips are made from sand, what makes a computer fast, why phones have special AI chips, and why countries compete to make them.
learn: What semiconductors are and why silicon is used
How transistors act as switches and make logic gates
How processing power and memory affect a computer's performance
The difference between CPUs, GPUs and AI chips
Why semiconductors matter to countries, the economy and the environment
intro: There are more transistors in your phone than there are people on Earth, and each one is made from purified sand. In this topic you'll find out how a semiconductor switch works, build logic with gates, follow a chip from sand to factory, work out what really makes a computer fast, and discover why microchips have become one of the most important industries on the planet.

pages.title: Switches made of sand
pages.spec: Explain what a semiconductor is and how a transistor works as a switch
pages.summary: Conductors let electricity flow and insulators don't; semiconductors such as silicon can be controlled to do either. A transistor is a tiny semiconductor switch: a small signal turns it on or off, which is how computers represent 1 and 0.
pages.starter: Name something that conducts electricity and something that doesn't. What would be useful about a material that could do both?
sc: I can describe conductors, insulators and semiconductors
I can explain why silicon is used for chips
I can explain how a transistor works as a switch

b: Conductors let electricity flow easily: copper, gold
Insulators block it: plastic, rubber, glass
Semiconductors are in between: we can control when they conduct
Silicon is the most widely used semiconductor
Silicon is the second most common element in the Earth's crust
Found in sand as silicon dioxide (quartz)
Purified to 99.9999999% pure for chips
Small amounts of other elements are added (doping) to control how it conducts
A transistor is a switch with no moving parts
A small voltage on its "gate" turns the flow of current on or off
On = 1, off = 0: transistors store and process bits
Modern chips contain billions of transistors

blocks.caption: How materials handle electricity
head: Type
What it does
Examples
rows: Conducts only under certain conditions, which we can control

blocks.text: Silicon

**[[silicon]]** is the element used for most chips. It's the second most common element in the Earth's crust and is found in ordinary sand. For chips it's purified until it's around 99.9999999% pure. Tiny amounts of other elements are then added in a process called **doping**, which gives fine control over how the silicon conducts.
The transistor

A **[[transistor]]** is a tiny electronic switch made from semiconductor material, with no moving parts. A small voltage applied to the transistor's **gate** controls whether current flows through it: on (1) or off (0). That's how computers store and process **bits**.

The first transistor was made in 1947. Today a single **[[microchip]]** (a chip or integrated circuit) can contain tens of billions of transistors, each far too small to see even with an ordinary microscope.
Before transistors, computers used glass valves (vacuum tubes) as switches. They were large, hot and often burned out, so early computers filled whole rooms.

blocks.title: Transistor switch
steps: Build the circuit on the circuit simulator (or with the kit) your teacher shows: a battery, a transistor, an LED and a push-button connected to the transistor's gate.
Press the button: what happens to the LED? Release it.
Record what "1" and "0" mean in your circuit.
Explain how millions of these switches could store information.

q.q: What happened when you pressed and released the button, and what do 1 and 0 represent?
q.a: Pressing put a small voltage on the gate, switching the transistor on so current flowed and the LED lit (1); releasing switched it off (0).

q.q: How could a chip use billions of these switches to store a photo?
q.a: Each switch stores one bit; groups of bits represent numbers for each pixel's colour, so billions of switches can store all the pixels of a photo.

practice.q: Explain the difference between a conductor and a semiconductor.
practice.a: A conductor lets electricity flow easily all the time (1); a semiconductor conducts only under certain conditions which can be controlled (1).

practice.q: Explain how a transistor represents binary data.
practice.a: It's a switch that can be on or off (1); on represents 1 and off represents 0 (1).

pages.title: Logic from switches
pages.spec: Describe how transistors are combined into AND, OR and NOT logic gates and complete truth tables
pages.summary: Combining transistors makes logic gates, which take binary inputs and produce an output. AND, OR and NOT gates, described with truth tables, are the building blocks of every processor.
pages.starter: The school alarm sounds if the fire button is pressed OR smoke is detected. The car starts if the key is in AND the brake is pressed. What's the difference?
sc: I can describe AND, OR and NOT gates
I can combine gates to solve a simple problem

b: A logic gate takes one or more binary inputs and gives one output
Built from a few transistors
AND: output 1 only if BOTH inputs are 1
OR: output 1 if EITHER input is 1
NOT: flips the input (1 becomes 0)
A truth table lists every possible input and the output for each
Two inputs means 4 rows: 00, 01, 10, 11
Three inputs means 8 rows
Engineers use them to check circuits do what they should
Combine gates to make decisions: "alarm ON if door open AND alarm set"
Thousands of gates make an adder that can do sums
Billions make a processor
The same logic appears in programming: if (a && b)

blocks.text: Logic gates

A **[[logic gate]]** is a small circuit, built from a few transistors, that takes one or more binary inputs (0 or 1) and produces one output. This kind of true/false logic is called **[[Boolean]]** logic, after the mathematician George Boole.
Truth tables
A **[[truth table]]** shows the output for every possible combination of inputs.

blocks.caption: OR gate: output 1 if either input (or both) is 1

blocks.text: Combining gates

blocks.title: A smart alarm
blocks.context: An alarm should sound (output 1) if the alarm is SET and either the DOOR or the WINDOW is open.
steps: Combine DOOR and WINDOW with an OR gate: 1 if either is open.
Combine that result with SET using an AND gate.
Logic: ALARM = SET AND (DOOR OR WINDOW).
blocks.answer: If SET = 1, DOOR = 0, WINDOW = 1, then DOOR OR WINDOW = 1, and 1 AND 1 = 1, so the alarm sounds.

blocks.text: You use the same logic in programming. In C#, AND is &&, OR is || and NOT is !.

blocks.title: Logic gate challenges
steps: Use the logic gate simulator your teacher shows (e.g. an online circuit builder).
Build and test AND, OR and NOT gates, completing a truth table for each.
Build the smart alarm: ALARM = SET AND (DOOR OR WINDOW). Test all 8 input combinations.
Extension: design a circuit for "the light comes on if it's dark AND movement is detected".

q.q: Complete the truth table for the smart alarm for these rows: SET=0, DOOR=1, WINDOW=1; SET=1, DOOR=0, WINDOW=0; SET=1, DOOR=1, WINDOW=0.
q.a: 0 (alarm not set); 0 (nothing open); 1 (set and door open).

q.q: Write the logic for the extension and explain it.
q.a: LIGHT = DARK AND MOVEMENT: the light only switches on when both are 1, saving electricity in daylight.

practice.a: AND gate (1), because both conditions must be true for the output to be 1 (1).

pages.title: From sand to chip
pages.spec: Describe the main stages of microchip manufacture
pages.summary: Chips are made in ultra-clean factories called fabs. Silicon is purified and grown into crystals, sliced into wafers, then patterns are printed onto it with light in many layers (photolithography), before the chips are tested, cut and packaged.

blocks.text: Making a microchip
Chips are made in factories called **[[fab|fabs]]** (fabrication plants), some of the most advanced and expensive buildings ever built.

items: **Purify.** Silicon is extracted from quartz sand and purified.
**Grow.** Molten silicon is slowly pulled into a large single crystal called an ingot.
**Slice.** The ingot is sliced into thin discs called **[[wafer|wafers]]** and polished until they're perfectly smooth.
**Pattern.** Circuit patterns are printed onto the wafer using light (photolithography), then etched. This is repeated for dozens of layers.
**Test and package.** Each chip on the wafer is tested, the wafer is cut up, and working chips are sealed in protective packages with connectors.

blocks.text: Photolithography

**[[photolithography]]** prints circuit patterns using light, a bit like projecting a stencil. A wafer is coated with a light-sensitive material; light shining through a patterned mask changes the coating where it lands; chemicals then remove the exposed (or unexposed) parts, and the pattern is etched into the layer underneath. The most advanced chips are made with **extreme ultraviolet (EUV)** light, which has a very short wavelength so it can print incredibly tiny features.
Clean rooms and tiny sizes

A single speck of dust is far bigger than a transistor, so chips are made in **[[clean room|clean rooms]]**, where the air is constantly filtered and workers wear full-body suits. Chip features are measured in **[[nanometre|nanometres]]** (nm): one nanometre is a billionth of a metre. A human hair is about 80,000 nm wide; the smallest chip features are just a few nanometres to tens of nanometres.
Chip "process names" like "3 nm" are mainly marketing labels for each new generation; they no longer measure one exact part of the transistor. But the features really are astonishingly small.

blocks.title: Chip factory flowchart

q.a: Purify silicon; grow ingot; slice into wafers; photolithography and etching (repeated for many layers); test; cut and package.

q.q: Why must chips be made in clean rooms?
q.a: The features are far smaller than dust particles, so a single speck of dust landing on a wafer could block or break a circuit and ruin the chip.

pages.title: What makes a computer fast?
pages.spec: Explain how processing power and memory capacity affect a computer's performance
pages.summary: Performance depends on the processor (clock speed, number of cores, cache) and on memory (how much RAM and how fast storage is). Moore's law described how the number of transistors on chips doubled about every two years, making computers ever more powerful.
pages.starter: Two laptops cost the same. One has a faster processor; the other has twice the RAM. Which would you pick for video editing? For lots of browser tabs?
sc: I can explain clock speed, cores and cache
I can explain how RAM and storage affect performance

b: Clock speed: instructions processed per second, in gigahertz (GHz); 3 GHz = 3 billion cycles a second
Cores: separate processors on one chip that work at the same time
Cache: tiny, super-fast memory inside the processor
More cores help only if the software can split up its work
RAM holds the programs and data in use right now
Too little RAM: the computer slows down as it swaps data to storage
Storage (SSD/hard drive) keeps files when the power is off
SSDs are much faster than hard drives, so computers start quicker
Gordon Moore (1965): the number of transistors on a chip doubles about every two years
Held for about 50 years: from thousands to tens of billions of transistors
Now slowing, as transistors approach the size of atoms
Engineers now stack chips in 3D and design specialised chips instead

blocks.text: The processor
The processor (CPU) carries out instructions. Three things affect how fast it is:

blocks.caption: Processor performance
head: Factor
What it means
Effect
rows: Number of cycles per second, measured in gigahertz (GHz)
Higher speed = more instructions per second
Separate processing units on one chip
More cores = more tasks at once (if software can use them)
Small, very fast memory inside the processor
More cache = less waiting for data from RAM

blocks.text: Memory and storage

**[[RAM]]** (random access memory) holds the programs and data being used right now. If you open more than fits in RAM, the computer has to swap data back and forth with storage, which slows it down. **Storage**, such as a solid-state drive (SSD) or hard disk, keeps files permanently. SSDs have no moving parts and are much faster than hard disks.

blocks.title: Choosing a laptop
blocks.context: Laptop A: 4 cores, 3.5 GHz, 8 GB RAM. Laptop B: 8 cores, 3.0 GHz, 16 GB RAM. Same price.
steps: Video editing uses many cores and lots of RAM for large files.
Laptop B has twice the cores and twice the RAM; its slightly lower clock speed matters less.
For simple tasks like web browsing, both are fine, but B handles many tabs better thanks to more RAM.
blocks.answer: Laptop B is the better choice for video editing and multitasking.

blocks.text: Moore's law

In 1965, Gordon Moore, who later co-founded Intel, predicted that the number of transistors on a chip would double about every two years. This prediction, **[[Moore's law]]**, held for roughly 50 years: early chips had a few thousand transistors; today's largest have tens of billions. It's why your phone is far more powerful than room-sized computers from the past. Moore's law is now slowing as transistors approach the size of a few atoms, so engineers stack chips in 3D and design chips for specific jobs.

blocks.title: Spec detective
steps: Your teacher gives you the specs of four devices (a gaming PC, a school laptop, a phone and a 10-year-old desktop).
Rank them for three tasks: video editing, web browsing with 30 tabs, and a 3D game.
Justify each ranking using clock speed, cores, cache, RAM and storage.

q.q: Which device is best for video editing, and which specifications support your choice?
q.a: Usually the gaming PC: most cores, high clock speed, lots of RAM and a fast SSD to handle large video files.

q.q: Explain why the 10-year-old desktop might feel slow even for web browsing.
q.a: It probably has little RAM and a slow hard disk, so modern websites with lots of tabs don't fit in memory and the computer swaps data to slow storage.

What is a core?
o: A separate processing unit on a chip

check.q: What happens if a computer runs out of RAM?
o: It slows down as it swaps data to storage

check.q: What did Moore's law predict?
o: Transistor counts on chips would double about every two years

practice.q: Explain how clock speed, number of cores and cache size affect processor performance.
practice.a: Higher clock speed = more instructions per second (1); more cores = more tasks in parallel (1); more cache = faster access to frequently used data/less waiting (1).

practice.q: Explain why adding more RAM can make a computer faster.
practice.a: More programs/data can be held in RAM at once (1), so less slow swapping with storage (1).

pages.title: CPUs, GPUs and AI chips
pages.spec: Compare CPUs, GPUs and AI accelerators and explain why specialised chips are increasingly used
pages.summary: CPUs are flexible all-rounders; GPUs have thousands of simple cores that are brilliant at doing the same sum many times at once, which suits graphics and AI. Phones now contain a system on a chip with a CPU, GPU and an AI processor (NPU) all together.
pages.starter: Would you rather have one genius mathematician or 1,000 pupils who can each do simple sums? Which would be quicker at marking 1,000 times-table tests?
sc: I can compare a CPU and a GPU
I can explain why GPUs are used for AI
I can describe a system on a chip

b: CPU: a few powerful cores, good at complex, varied tasks one after another
GPU: thousands of simpler cores doing the same calculation on lots of data at once
Parallel processing: many calculations at the same time
Graphics: millions of pixels, same maths for each, so perfect for GPUs
Training AI means trillions of simple multiplications
GPUs turned out to be brilliant at this, so demand for them exploded
Companies now design AI accelerators specifically for machine learning
Phones have an NPU (neural processing unit) for on-device AI
A phone's main chip combines CPU, GPU, NPU, memory controllers and more
Called a system on a chip (SoC)
Saves space and power, which is vital for battery life
Many are based on designs from Arm, a UK company in Cambridge

blocks.text: CPUs and GPUs

blocks.caption: CPU or GPU?
head: Feature
CPU
GPU
rows: Complex, varied tasks one after another
The same calculation on huge amounts of data at once
Running the operating system, apps, logic

blocks.text: A **[[CPU]]** is a flexible all-rounder. A **[[GPU]]** was originally designed for graphics: drawing a game frame means doing the same maths for millions of pixels, so a GPU does them all at once. This is called **[[parallel processing]]**.
Why AI needs special chips

Training and running AI models involves trillions of simple multiplications that can be done in parallel, exactly what GPUs are good at. As AI boomed, demand for powerful GPUs soared, making their designers among the most valuable companies in the world. Companies now also build **AI accelerators** designed only for machine learning. Phones and laptops include an **[[NPU]]** (neural processing unit) so AI features like face unlock, live translation and photo enhancement can run on the device instead of in the cloud, which is faster and more private.
System on a chip

A phone has no room for separate CPU, GPU and memory chips, so they're combined into one **[[system on a chip]]** (SoC). This saves space and power, which is vital for battery life. Many of the world's SoCs, in phones, tablets and even some laptops and data centres, use processor designs from **Arm**, a British company based in Cambridge.

blocks.title: Who's the best worker?
steps: Activity 1: one volunteer (the "CPU") solves 30 simple sums alone while the rest of the class (the "GPU") solves them with one sum each. Time both.
Activity 2: the CPU solves one multi-step logic puzzle; the GPU class must each do one step without talking to each other. Time both.
Record which "processor" won each round and why.

q.q: Which processor won each round, and why?
q.a: The GPU class won the simple sums because everyone worked in parallel; the CPU won the logic puzzle because each step depended on the last, so it couldn't be split up.

q.q: Explain why GPUs are used to train AI models.
q.a: Training AI involves huge numbers of simple calculations that can be done at the same time, which suits a GPU's thousands of parallel cores.

check.q: What is a GPU best at?
o: Running one complex task step by step
Doing the same calculation on lots of data at once

check.q: What is parallel processing?
o: Doing many calculations at the same time

check.q: What is an NPU?
o: A neural processing unit designed for AI tasks

check.q: What is a system on a chip?
o: One chip combining CPU, GPU and other parts
A chip with a tiny operating system

practice.q: Compare a CPU and a GPU.
practice.a: CPU has a few powerful cores (1) suited to complex/varied tasks one after another (1); GPU has thousands of simpler cores suited to parallel tasks like graphics/AI (1).

practice.q: Give two advantages of running AI on a phone's NPU instead of in the cloud.
practice.a: Any two: faster/no waiting for the internet (1); works offline (1); more private as data stays on the phone (1); uses less data (1).

pages.title: The global chip race
pages.spec: Explain why semiconductors matter to the economy, national security and the environment
pages.summary: Chips are in almost everything, and making them depends on a few companies in a few countries. Shortages can halt car factories, so governments invest to secure supplies. Chip-making also uses huge amounts of energy and water.
pages.starter: In 2021, car factories around the world stopped building cars because of a shortage of something tiny. What was it?

I can explain why governments see chips as a security issue
I can describe environmental impacts of chip-making

b: Designers (e.g. Arm in the UK, Nvidia and Apple in the US) create chip designs
Machine makers (ASML in the Netherlands) build the lithography tools
Foundries (e.g. TSMC in Taiwan, Samsung in South Korea) manufacture chips
Packaging and testing often happen in other countries again

A disaster or conflict there could disrupt the whole world's technology
The US, EU and others have spent tens of billions of pounds building new fabs
The UK's strategy focuses on chip design, research and compound semiconductors

blocks.text: A global supply chain
A **[[supply chain]]** is every step and company involved in making a product. Chips have one of the most complicated supply chains in the world:

blocks.caption: Who does what?
head: Stage
Example companies and countries
rows: ASML (Netherlands), the only maker of EUV machines
Often in Taiwan, Malaysia, China and other countries

blocks.text: The chip shortage

From 2020 to 2022 the world faced a **[[chip shortage]]**. During the pandemic, demand for laptops and games consoles soared while factories shut and supply chains were disrupted. Car makers, whose cars contain hundreds of chips, had to stop production lines, and millions fewer cars were built. The shortage showed how much the modern world depends on chips.
Chips and national security

Most of the world's most advanced chips are made by one company, TSMC, in Taiwan. Because chips are vital for everything from phones to fighter jets, governments see them as a matter of **national security**. The United States and the European Union have committed tens of billions to new fabs. The UK's National Semiconductor Strategy (2023) focuses on its strengths: chip design (such as Arm), research, and compound semiconductors, with a major cluster in South Wales.
The environment

Chip fabs use enormous amounts of electricity and ultra-pure water, and handle hazardous chemicals and gases. And when devices are replaced quickly, the result is **[[e-waste]]**, electronic waste that contains both toxic materials and valuable metals.

blocks.title: Greener chips, greener habits
items: Chip makers are switching to renewable energy and recycling water
More efficient chips use less power, which helps phones and data centres
Keep devices longer, repair them, and recycle them properly

q.q: Write the proposal your class voted for and explain why it would help.
q.a: E.g. "Countries agree to share chip stockpiles in emergencies and fund fabs powered by renewable energy, reducing the risk of shortages and the environmental impact."

practice.q: Explain why governments see semiconductors as a national security issue.
practice.a: Chips are vital for everything including defence/infrastructure (1), and most advanced chips are made in very few places, so supply could be disrupted (1).
